page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: Lewis acid
lines: Lewis acid: a substance that can accept a
lone pair of electrons.
Example: BF₃ (the boron atom has only six
valence electrons, so it can accept a lone
pair).
steps.why: The Lewis theory defines acid and base by electron pairs, not by protons. Acceptor of a lone pair is the whole definition, and BF₃ is the standard example because boron's octet is incomplete.
common_mistakes: Writing proton donor. That is the Brønsted-Lowry acid, not the Lewis acid.
Writing electron acceptor without the word pair. The acid accepts a lone PAIR of electrons.
steps.memory_tip: Acid Accepts the pair — both words start with A.
steps.margin_note: Electron-pair acceptor, never proton donor — the theories must not mix.

steps.label: Types of Lewis acids
lines: a) Simple cations: Ag⁺, Co³⁺
b) Molecules whose central atom has an
incomplete octet: BF₃, BCl₃
c) Molecules with multiple bonds between
atoms of different electronegativity:
CO₂, SO₂
steps.why: Each type is a different reason the substance can take a lone pair: a positive charge, an empty place in the octet, or a multiple bond that can shift its electrons aside.
common_mistakes: Listing anions such as Cl⁻ as Lewis acids. Anions hold extra electrons, so they are bases.
Giving the types without one example each. The examples carry the mark with the list.
steps.memory_tip: Three ways to have room for a pair: positive charge, empty octet, shiftable multiple bond.
steps.margin_note: Three labelled types, one example each.

steps.label: Lewis base and its types
lines: Lewis base: a substance that can donate a
lone pair of electrons.
a) Simple anions: Cl⁻, OH⁻
b) Molecules with lone pairs on the central
atom: H₂O, NH₃
c) Molecules with multiple bonds: CO, NO
steps.why: The base is the mirror of the acid: it has a lone pair available and gives it into the new bond. Anions and lone-pair molecules are the two common ways to have a spare pair.
common_mistakes: Writing proton acceptor. That is the Brønsted-Lowry base; the Lewis base donates an electron pair.
Swapping donor and acceptor between acid and base.
steps.memory_tip: Base gives the pair. NH₃ and H₂O, the everyday bases, both carry visible lone pairs.
steps.margin_note: Definition plus the three types with examples.

steps.label: Neutralisation
lines: Neutralisation in this theory is the
formation of a coordinate covalent bond
between the base and the acid.
(the oxygen atom donates its lone pair
to H⁺)

lines.text: Lewis acid = lone-pair acceptor; Lewis base = lone-pair donor

steps.why: The two definitions meet in the bond: the base's lone pair becomes the shared pair of a coordinate covalent bond, and that bond formation is what the theory calls neutralisation.
common_mistakes: Describing neutralisation as acid + base giving salt + water. In the Lewis theory it is the formation of a coordinate bond.
Forgetting to name which species donates the pair in the example.
steps.memory_tip: Neutralisation = one new coordinate bond. The base's lone pair becomes the shared pair.
steps.margin_note: Close with the boxed acceptor/donor pair — the two definitions side by side.
